{{For|the recent championship|World Rapid Chess Championship 2025}}
[[File:Magnus_Carlsen_in_2025.jpg|thumb|right|[[Magnus Carlsen]], the current World Rapid Champion.]]
[[File:Aleksandra Goryachkina Russian Superfinal 2024 03 (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|[[Aleksandra Goryachkina]], the current Women's World Rapid Champion.]]
The '''World Rapid Chess Championship''' is a [[chess tournament]] held to determine the world champion in [[rapid chess]]. Prior to 2012, [[FIDE]] sporadically sanctioned a world rapid chess championship. Meanwhile, the non-FIDE-recognized [[#Grenkeleasing Rapid World Championship|Grenkeleasing Rapid World Championship]] annually named a world rapid champion of its own each year from 1996 to 2010. Since 2012, FIDE has held an annual joint rapid and [[World Blitz Chess Championship|blitz tournament]], billed as the World Rapid & Blitz Chess Championships. FIDE also holds the Women's World Rapid & Blitz Chess Championship. 

The current rapid world champion is [[Grandmaster (Chess)|GM]] [[Magnus Carlsen]] of [[Norway]]. GM [[Aleksandra Goryachkina]] of [[Russia]] is the current women's rapid world champion. GM [[Viswanathan Anand|Vishwanathan Anand]] of [[India]] holds the record for most championship wins, having won 13 World Rapid titles.

==History==

[[File:Mazatlan 1988 Active Chess Championship.png|thumb|240px|Advertisement for 1988 World Active Chess Championship]]

The concept of rapid chess (then called "active chess") made its debut at a 1987 FIDE Congress meeting in [[Seville]], Spain. The first official high-profile rapid match took place later that year, when then-world champion [[Garry Kasparov]] defeated [[Nigel Short]] in the "London Docklands Speed Chess Challenge" at the [[London Hippodrome]]. Kasparov won the match with 4 wins, two losses, and no draws in six games.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/4th-april-1987/52/chess |title=The Spectator: 3 APRIL 1987, Page 52 |access-date=3 January 2017 |archive-date=24 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624112519/http://archive.spectator.co.uk/article/4th-april-1987/52/chess |url-status=live }}</ref>

During the World Active Chess Championship the following year, time controls were set at 30 minutes per player per game.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://worldchess.com/2016/12/25/a-brief-history-of-fast-chess/ |title=A Brief History of Fast Chess |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2017-01-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103172317/https://worldchess.com/2016/12/25/a-brief-history-of-fast-chess/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1993, following his split from FIDE, world champion [[Garry Kasparov]] organized a slightly quicker version of active chess, dubbing it "rapid chess". The [[Professional Chess Association]], Kasparov's competitor to FIDE, subsequently organized two Grand Prix cycles of rapid chess before folding in 1996. Under rapid chess time controls, each player was allowed 25 minutes with an additional 10 seconds after each move.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9IfLBWWNgZgC&q=%22professional+chess+association%22+%22rapid%22+%22grand+prix%22+%22kasparov%22&pg=PA276|title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to Chess|isbn=9781101221952|last1=Wolff|first1=Patrick|date=September 2001|access-date=2020-11-04|archive-date=2021-12-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228214417/https://books.google.com/books?id=9IfLBWWNgZgC&q=%22professional+chess+association%22+%22rapid%22+%22grand+prix%22+%22kasparov%22&pg=PA276|url-status=live}}</ref> FIDE would adopt these time controls and the "rapid chess" moniker for the rapid tiebreak stages of the [[FIDE World Chess Championship 1999|1999 FIDE World Chess Championship]].

In 2012, FIDE inaugurated the World Rapid & Blitz Chess Championships, holding the World Rapid Championship alongside the [[World Blitz Chess Championship|World Blitz Championship]]. The current time controls for the rapid event is 15 minutes per player with a 10 second increment.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/WorldRapidBlitzChampionshipsRegulations.pdf |title=Regulations for the FIDE World Rapid Championship 2015 |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2017-12-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171208034648/https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/WorldRapidBlitzChampionshipsRegulations.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Grenkeleasing Rapid World Championship ==

[[Image:Anand-Kasparov 2000-06-24 Frankfurt.jpg|thumb|Viswanathan Anand and Garry Kasparov face off in the 2000 edition of the championship]]

Starting in 1994, the Mainz [[Chess Classic]] was an annual series of tournaments hosted by the ''Chess Tigers'' in [[Mainz]], Germany. The brainchild of Hans-Walter Schmitt, the Chess Classic featured top-ranked players playing rapid and [[Fischer Random chess]] games against computers as well as each other. The main event of the classic was the '''Grenkeleasing Rapid World Championship''' (formerly Fujitsu-Siemens), a tournament generally considered as the traditional rapid chess championship in the absence of an annual FIDE-recognized championship.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gambit.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/08/20/anand-wins-rapid-championship-at-mainz-navara-wins-open/?_r=0 |title=NYTimes.com - Anand Wins Rapid Championship at Mainz; Navara Wins Open}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.chess.com/uk/news/aronian-wins-rapid-world-championship-8519 |title=Chess.com - Aronian Wins Rapid World Championship |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2017-01-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103170652/https://www.chess.com/uk/news/aronian-wins-rapid-world-championship-8519 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chesstigers.de/alte_daten/chesstigers_alt/ChessClassic/ChessClassic2000e/Home/preview.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118135135/http://www.chesstigers.de/alte_daten/chesstigers_alt/ChessClassic/ChessClassic2000e/Home/preview.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=2017-01-18 |title=Preview: Frankfurt Chess Classic 2000}}</ref> Indian grandmaster [[Viswanathan Anand]] holds the record for most championship wins, having won the event 11 times in 15 years — including 9 consecutive victories from 2000 to 2008.

From 1996 to 1998, the Rapid Chess Championship at [[Frankfurt]] was organized as a double-round robin, followed by a match between the 1st and 2nd-place finishers for the championship. With the addition of Karpov to the field in 1999, the format was temporarily changed to a pure round-robin, with the 1st-place finisher winning the championship. The following year the field was expanded further to include all ten of the top 10-rated Grandmasters in the world, and was dubbed a Category 21 tournament with an average Elo rating of 2767.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/mainz-2009-schmitt-i-suffer-vicariously-with-anand- |title=CB News: Mainz 2009 – Schmitt: 'I suffer vicariously with Anand' |access-date=2017-01-07 |archive-date=2017-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108190233/https://en.chessbase.com/post/mainz-2009-schmitt-i-suffer-vicariously-with-anand- |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2001 the event moved to [[Mainz]], and shifted from a round-robin to a matchplay format - the defending champion Viswanathan Anand defended his title in an eight-game match against the winner of the previous year's Ordix Open, the open rapid tournament. In 2007, with Anand still the rapid champion after six successful title defenses, the event reverted to a double-round robin tournament, with the top two finishers in the semi-finals advancing to the finals.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mark-weeks.com/aboutcom/mw01a01.htm |title=Viswanathan Anand's Tournament, Match, and Exhibition Record (1983-) |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2017-01-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170104000143/http://www.mark-weeks.com/aboutcom/mw01a01.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> In a homage to the [[Masters Tournament]], the winner of the championship is traditionally awarded a winner's black jacket.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scrkuppenheim.de/meko/frankfurt.html |title=Frankfurt puts everything which has gone before in the shade |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2013-12-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131205011825/http://www.scrkuppenheim.de/meko/frankfurt.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2010, the event's final year, the Open GRENKE Rapid Championship featured a field of over 700 players. Shortly afterwards, the ''Chess Tigers'' withdrew financial backing for the event, due in part to the effects of the [[2008 financial crisis]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/che-claic-mainz-end-of-an-era |title=CB News: Chess Classic Mainz – End of an Era |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2019-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190504094509/https://en.chessbase.com/post/che-claic-mainz-end-of-an-era |url-status=live }}</ref>

==FIDE-recognized events==

=== Pre-2012 ===
Prior to 2012, FIDE sporadically sanctioned a world rapid chess championship, organizing just three such events. These occurred in 1988, 2001, and 2003. Each of the events was a [[multi-stage tournament]] with a preliminary stage followed by an eight-player [[Single-elimination tournament|single-elimination]] to determine the winner.

===World Rapid & Blitz Chess Championships (since 2012)===

On May 31, 2012, FIDE announced the inaugural World Rapid & Blitz Championships, set to take place in [[Astana]], Kazakhstan from July 1 to 11. The 2012 tournament consisted of a qualifying round, followed by the rapid and blitz events held consecutively over 5 days. In order to promote viewership, time controls were set at 15 minutes per player, rather than the pre-2012 standard of 25 minutes. The championship was originally structured as a 16-player [[round-robin tournament]], set to coincide with the first release of FIDE's rapid and blitz ratings in July 2012; invited were the top 10 players in the FIDE ratings list, the three medalists of the qualification competition, and three wild-card nominees by the organization committee and FIDE.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/Regulations_World_Rapid_2012.pdf |title=Regulations for the World Rapid Chess Championship 2012 |access-date=2017-01-03 |archive-date=2013-03-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130308224127/http://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/Regulations_World_Rapid_2012.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2013, the format was changed to a [[Swiss tournament]] with a field of over 100 grandmasters. The top three finishers in the standings are awarded gold, silver, and bronze medals respectively.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chess.com (News) |date=2013-06-08 |title=Mamedyarov wins FIDE World Rapid Championship |url=https://www.chess.com/news/view/mamedyarov-wins-fide-world-rapid-championship-7062 |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Chess.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Various methods of resolving [[Tie-breaking in Swiss-system tournaments|ties]] have been used and the 2016 edition resulted in all three medallists tied on 11/15 points with the champion being determined by comparing the average rating of each player's opponents. From 2017 onwards, a tie-breaker match has been played in the event of two or more players being tied on points for first place.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/wrbc_regulations_2017_open.pdf |title=Regulations for the FIDE World Rapid Championship 2017 |access-date=2021-12-28 |archive-date=2021-12-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211229154450/https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/wrbc_regulations_2017_open.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Only two players may participate in this match, even where three or more players are tied for first place on points. This caused some controversy in the 2021 edition where four players tied for 1st with a score of 9.5/13. A tie-break match for the gold and silver medals was held between [[Nodirbek Abdusattorov]] and [[Ian Nepomniachtchi]] due to having the highest [[Buchholz system|Buchholz]] (Cut 1) scores of the four players. [[Magnus Carlsen]], the defending champion, and [[Fabiano Caruana]] were therefore unable to participate in the tie-break match despite having the same score as the champion. Carlsen criticised this result as 'idiotic' and called for changes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nrk.no/sport/carlsen-mener-vm-regel-er-_idiotisk__-tapte-gullet-i-siste-parti-1.15788525 |title=Carlsen thinks World Cup rule is 'idiotic': Lost gold in last game |access-date=2021-12-28 |archive-date=2021-12-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211228205458/https://www.nrk.no/sport/carlsen-mener-vm-regel-er-_idiotisk__-tapte-gullet-i-siste-parti-1.15788525 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Other events ==

===ACP World Rapid Cup===

Starting in 2007, the [[Association of Chess Professionals]] (ACP) sponsored an annual event billed as the '''ACP World Rapid Cup'''. The 1st edition of the event was a 16-player [[Single-elimination tournament|knockout tournament]], jointly organized by the Pivdenny Bank of [[Ukraine]] and the [[Association of Chess Professionals|ACP]] and held in [[Odesa]], Ukraine at the Hotel Londonskaya from 4 January to 8 January 2007.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/first-acp-world-rapid-in-odea |title=First ACP World Rapid in Odessa |access-date=2018-01-31 |archive-date=2018-02-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201194529/https://en.chessbase.com/post/first-acp-world-rapid-in-odea |url-status=live }}</ref> The brainchild of Pivdenny Bank chairman and ACP president Vadim Morokhovsky,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.chessbase.com/post/3rd-acp-world-rapid-cup-in-odea |title=ChessBase News - 3rd ACP World Rapid Cup in Odessa |access-date=2018-01-31 |archive-date=2018-02-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201192948/https://en.chessbase.com/post/3rd-acp-world-rapid-cup-in-odea |url-status=live }}</ref> the tournament included the top finishers in each year's ACP Tour, a system in which participating players were ranked based on their performances in several chess tournaments held around the world. The remaining participants were chosen on a wildcard basis at the organizers' discretion. From 2007 to 2010, the tournament was held on an annual basis, with the 5th edition of the cup held in 2013.

Despite the ACP Cup's status as a non-FIDE event, [[FIDE Presidents|FIDE President]] [[Kirsan Ilyumzhinov]] was present at the inaugural edition of the tournament and took part in the opening ceremony.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fide.com/component/content/article/4-tournaments/1892-383-peter-leko-of-hungary-wins-the-1st-acp-world-rapid-cup.html |title=FIDE Report - Peter Leko of Hungary wins the 1st ACP World Rapid Cup |access-date=2018-01-31 |archive-date=2018-02-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201075552/https://www.fide.com/component/content/article/4-tournaments/1892-383-peter-leko-of-hungary-wins-the-1st-acp-world-rapid-cup.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> A subsequent agreement between [[FIDE]] and the ACP ensured that ACP would be able to use the title "World" when promoting and referring to the tournament.

Time controls were set at 20 minutes per player, with an increment of five seconds. Each match consisted of two rapid games, with the winner progressing to the next round. Ties were resolved by two blitz games, followed by a sudden-death [[Armageddon chess|armageddon]] game. The final match initially consisted of four rapid games, with the same tiebreaks; in 2013, the final was shortened to two rapid games.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.chessbase.com/(X(1)S(llg5s3n25xhqbvopexo5w3mx))/post/acp-03-grischuk-prevails-170913 |title=ChessBase News - ACP 2003: Grischuk prevails |access-date=2018-01-31 |archive-date=2018-02-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180201193008/https://en.chessbase.com/(X(1)S(llg5s3n25xhqbvopexo5w3mx))/post/acp-03-grischuk-prevails-170913 |url-status=live }}</ref>
